opus-5.5.text:
I think that claim is partly right, but we need to be careful about what we mean by "reaction."

PD control, proportional-derivative control, is a very low-level mechanism. You give a target position for a joint, and the controller computes a torque based on how far you are from the target and how fast you're moving. So if someone pushes the robot's arm, the error grows, and the controller automatically pushes back. In that sense, yes, it looks like a reflex. It's like a spring with a damper. It responds instantly, at maybe a thousand hertz, without any thinking.

And this is actually very important. A lot of people assume the neural network policy directly outputs torques and handles everything. In reality, in most of today's humanoid and quadruped systems, including the ones trained with reinforcement learning in simulation, the policy runs at maybe fifty hertz and outputs target joint positions. Then the PD controller underneath does the fast work. So the compliance, the smoothness, the ability to absorb small disturbances: a big part of that comes from the PD layer, not from the "intelligence."

But I wouldn't call it true reaction in the sense of intelligence. A spinal reflex in a human is still shaped by evolution and by the context the brain sets. PD control has no understanding. It doesn't know whether the push came from a person who wants a handshake or from a wall it's about to crash into. It just treats every deviation the same way, according to the gains you tuned. If the gains are high, the robot becomes stiff and can be dangerous; if they're low, it becomes floppy and can't do precise tasks. Choosing that trade-off is still a human decision, or something the upper-level policy has to learn to compensate for.

So my view is: PD control gives the robot a mechanical reflex, a kind of physical intuition baked into the hardware loop. That's a very useful foundation, and honestly it's one reason why sim-to-real works as well as it does. But real reaction, adapting how you respond based on what you perceive and what you're trying to do, has to come from the layers above. Maybe in the future, with variable impedance or policies that also output the gains, the boundary between the "reflex" and the "brain" will become blurrier, and that's a direction I find quite exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes PD control as a low-level controller with tuned gains and no understanding, but it does not state that PD control is not data-driven.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that framing is actually quite apt, and it's worth unpacking why. PD control, proportional-derivative control, is at its core a very simple idea. You have a target position for a joint, you compare it to where the joint actually is, and the error drives the torque. The proportional term pushes you back toward the target, and the derivative term damps the motion so you don't overshoot. That's it. There's no model of the world, no planning, no understanding of what's happening.

But when you watch a legged robot stand on a PD controller and someone shoves it, the behavior looks remarkably like a reflex. The leg gives a little, then pushes back. It happens in milliseconds, far faster than any high-level policy could deliberate. And that's exactly what a reaction is in biological systems too. When a doctor taps your knee, the response doesn't go through your brain. It's a local loop in the spinal cord. The muscle spindle senses a stretch, and the muscle contracts. That's essentially a proportional controller on muscle length, with some damping thrown in.

So I'd say the analogy holds at the level of function. PD control gives the robot a low-level layer that responds to disturbances before anything smarter has time to think. In most of the humanoid and quadruped work we do, the learned policy outputs target joint positions at maybe fifty hertz, and then PD runs underneath at something like a thousand hertz, turning those targets into torques. The policy decides where to go, and the PD layer handles the moment-to-moment pushing and pulling against gravity, contact, and surprises.

Where I'd push back a little is on the word "kind of." People sometimes hear "reaction" and imagine the robot is doing something intelligent at that layer. It isn't. The stiffness and damping gains are fixed numbers. If you tune them too high, the robot becomes rigid and brittle, and it will fight every contact and chatter. If you tune them too low, it goes mushy and can't hold a pose. The interesting part, in my view, is that the learned policy actually learns to exploit this layer. During training in simulation, the policy figures out that it can set a target slightly beyond where it wants the joint to end up, knowing the PD controller will produce a certain force. So the reaction isn't just a passive safety net. It becomes part of how the policy expresses itself. The two layers co-adapt, even though only one of them is learning.

So yes, PD gives a robot something like a reflex. But the real story is how a learned brain learns to live on top of a dumb spinal cord.

r001.rationale: The response describes the PD gains as fixed and says only the learned policy is learning, communicating that PD control itself is not data-driven.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a reasonable way to describe it, as long as we’re clear about what “reaction” means. A PD controller compares the robot’s current state with a target. The proportional term responds to the position error, and the derivative term responds to how quickly that error is changing. So if you push a robot’s joint away from its target, the controller adjusts the torque to bring it back, while damping the motion.

That is a basic feedback reaction. But it doesn’t mean the robot understands the push or decides what to do about it. Whether it should resist, yield, or take a step requires something beyond that fixed control rule. PD control can help execute a behavior; it doesn’t, by itself, choose the behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes PD control as a fixed control rule, but does not clearly state that it is not data-driven.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s fair if by “reaction” we mean a basic feedback response. A PD controller looks at the difference between the desired state and the current state, and at how quickly that difference is changing. If you push a robot’s joint away from its target, the controller adjusts the torque to bring it back, while damping the motion. In that sense, it reacts to a disturbance.

But that’s a very specific kind of reaction. It doesn’t mean the robot understands why you pushed it or decides whether returning to that position is appropriate. The target and the feedback rule are already given. So PD control provides a basic mechanism for responding, but richer behavior depends on how the robot chooses its targets and adapts them to the situation.

r001.rationale: The response describes PD control as a feedback rule with a given target, but never states that it is not data-driven.
